div.head: ECf 11.2
div.ab: Et hanc libertatem habuit sancta ecclesia usque ad tempus Willelmi iunioris, qui de baronibus totius patrie auxilium petiit ad Normanniam retinendam de fratre suo Rodberto eunte in Ierusalem.
div.note: Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 636 (November 2026): read from the page images and checked against the scan’s own text layer, differences settled against the page.

note.seg: die Beinamen des Rothen und Kurzhose, die Retr. Wilhelm II. und Robert giebt, sind im 12. Jh. allgemein. Die Steuer von Mitte 1096 (vgl. Freeman Wil. Rufus I 556; Chronologie widerspricht also Prolog c) heisst beim Angelsächsischen Annalisten geld (welcher Name auch das Dänengeld und im 12. Jh. Staatssteuer allgemein bezeichnet), aber nicht Denageld. Vier Schill., auch für die Stiftsdomäne, sagt Chron. Abingdon II 38; vgl. Round Domesday stud. I 83; dass die Steuer uillanos, agricolas drückte, bestätigen Flor. Wig., Will. Malmesb., der (Reg. IV 318, Pont. V 271) auch den Protest meldet, wie Abingdon., Flor. den Jammer der Kirche.

the nicknames the Red and Curthose, which the Retractator gives William II and Robert, are general in the 12th century. The tax of mid-1096 (cf. Freeman, Wil. Rufus I 556; so the chronology contradicts the Prologue, note c) is called geld by the Anglo-Saxon annalist (a name that also denotes the Danegeld and, in the 12th century, state taxation in general), but not Denageld. Four shillings, also for the demesne of the minster, says Chron. Abingdon II 38; cf. Round, Domesday stud. I 83; that the tax weighed on uillanos, agricolas is confirmed by Flor. Wig. and Will. Malmesb., who (Reg. IV 318, Pont. V 271) also reports the protest, as Abingdon. and Flor. report the lament of the Church.

div.ab: And holy Church had this liberty until the time of William the younger, who sought aid from the barons of the whole country for retaining Normandy from his brother Robert, who was going to Jerusalem.
